title: Welcoming Tourists
hint: Greeting visitors and offering help; closed questions (Is this your first visit? Would you like a map or a guide?) and open questions (Where are you from? What would you like to see?)
why: when you work in a hotel, a shop, a café or as a guide, or when you just help a visitor in your town, the first minute matters. A warm welcome and the right questions make visitors feel at home, and small question mistakes like Where you are from? are easy to hear.
understand: closed to check, open to chat
able: greet a visitor and make them feel welcome
ask closed and open questions with the right word order
give simple information: opening times, distances and suggestions
mistakes: Where you are from?
Where are you from?
Do you are tired?
Are you tired?
How long you stay?
How long are you staying?
Did you enjoyed the tour?
Did you enjoy the tour? (after did, use the base verb)
What time opens the museum?
What time does the museum open?
Are you hungry? Yes, I do.
Are you hungry? Yes, I am. (answer with the same verb as the question)
warmup: Have you ever worked with tourists, or helped a visitor in your town? What did they ask you?
When you travel, what is the first question people usually ask you?
Which questions are easy for you in English? Which ones do you often get wrong?

rows: greeting a visitor when they arrive
Good evening, and welcome to the Harbour Hotel!
the first time you meet someone
Hi, I'm Sam, your guide for today. Nice to meet you.
How was your flight? Not too long, I hope.
offering help in a shop, hotel or café
Would you like a map of the city?
offering to take or show someone
Let me show you to your room.
The gallery is open from ten to six.
saying how far something is (no -s on minute)
The station? It's a five-minute walk from here.
saying goodbye to a guest or visitor

vocab.note: With customers and the public, the polite version sounds warmer and more professional. The grammar is the same; you add would, could, may or a softener.
rows: What can I get you? / How can I help you?
Could I have your name, please? / May I have your name?
Would you mind waiting a moment? / I'll be right with you.
I'm afraid it's closed today, but it opens at nine tomorrow.
I'm not sure, but I'll find out for you.
Is there anything else I can help you with?

helper verb + subject + verb ...?
(is, are, do, does, did, have, can, would)
Is this your first visit? Do you have a reservation? Can I take your coat?
check a fact quickly: the answer is yes or no
Would you like tea or coffee? Are you here for work or on holiday?

question word + helper verb + subject + verb ...?
(where, what, when, which, who, why, how long, how many)
Where are you from? How long are you staying? What would you like to see?
get people talking and find out more

vocab.note: Answer a closed question with the same helper verb. Just Yes or No can sound a little cold.
rows: Yes, I am. / Yes, we are.

vocab.h: Turn a closed question into an open one
vocab.note: A closed question can stop the conversation: Yes. Use a question word to keep it going.
rows: What did you enjoy most about the tour?
Is this your first time in Canada?
How are you finding the hotel?

say: In yes/no questions your voice usually goes up at the end: Is this your first visit? ↗ In open questions it usually goes down: Where are you from? ↘ In either/or questions it goes up, then down: Tea ↗ or coffee ↘?

exercises.title: Question and answer
exercises.intro: Match each question to the best answer. Tap a question, then tap the answer.

items.l: Is this your first visit to Toronto?
items.r: Yes, it is. We're very excited.
items.why: A yes/no question with is: answer with is. Yes, it is.

items.l: Are you staying for the weekend?
items.r: No, we aren't. We're here for a week.
items.why: A question with are needs are in the short answer: No, we aren't.

items.r: Yes, we do. It's under Garcia.
items.why: A question with do needs do in the answer: Yes, we do.

items.l: Would you like tea or coffee?
items.why: An either/or question: the answer is one of the choices, not yes or no.
Where asks about a place, so the answer is a place.

items.r: Five nights. We leave on Sunday.
items.why: How long asks about time: five nights, a week, until Sunday.

items.l: What would you like to see?
items.r: The CN Tower and the islands.
items.why: An open question with what: the answer gives information, not yes or no.
How was ...? asks for an opinion or description: fine, long, great.

items.post: you staying in the city centre?
items.why: With staying (be + -ing), use are: Are you staying ...?

items.post: you need a map of the city?
items.why: Need is a normal verb, so use do with you: Do you need a map?
Be from: Where are you from? (I am from ...)
Open is a normal verb and the museum is it, so use does: What time does the museum open?
Your journey = it, in the past: Was your journey OK?
With staying (be + -ing), use are: How long are you staying?
After did, use the base verb: Did you enjoy ...? Did already shows the past.

items.pre: Would you like a window table
items.why: An either/or question offers a choice: A or B?

items.post: you like me to call a taxi for you?
items.why: Would you like ...? is the polite way to offer something.

items.post: is your hotel? I can show you on the map.
items.why: Where asks about a place: Where is your hotel?

items.post: are you staying in Canada? Two weeks or longer?
items.why: How long asks about time: How long are you staying?

items.post: you been to Niagara Falls yet?
items.why: Have you been ...? asks about experience up to now (present perfect).

items.post: I help you with your bags?
items.why: Can I help you ...? offers help.
What time asks for a clock time: What time does the last bus leave?
How many + plural noun asks for a number: How many people?

items.post: tour would you prefer: the walking tour or the bus tour?
items.why: Which asks someone to choose from a small number of things.

items.answer: Is this your first time in Canada?
items.why: Yes/no question with be: Is + this + your first time ...?

items.answer: Where would you like to go tomorrow?
items.why: Open question: question word + would + you + like to go.

items.answer: Do you need help with your luggage?
items.why: Yes/no question: Do + you + need + the rest.

items.answer: How was your flight from London?
items.why: How was + subject (your flight) + the rest.
Question word + does + subject (breakfast) + base verb (start).

exercises.title: Reading
exercises.text:
At the front desk of the Maple Leaf Hostel, Toronto

Priya: Good evening, and welcome to the Maple Leaf Hostel! How was your journey?

Fiona: Long! Our flight from Glasgow was eight hours, and then we took the train from the airport.

Priya: Oh, you must be tired. Do you have a reservation?

Callum: Yes, we do. It's under MacLeod, for four nights.

Priya: Perfect. Here are your keys. You're in room 12, on the second floor. Breakfast is from seven to ten in the kitchen downstairs. Is this your first time in Toronto?

Fiona: Yes, it is. We don't know anything about the city!

Priya: Don't worry. What would you like to do while you're here?

Callum: We love music, and we'd like to see the lake.

Priya: Then take the ferry to the Toronto Islands. It's a twenty-minute walk to the ferry terminal from here. And there's live jazz at a bar on Queen Street every Friday. Would you like a map?

Fiona: Yes, please. Thank you so much!
exercises.intro: Read the conversation. Look at Priya's questions: which are closed and which are open? Then type the missing word from the text, and press Check.

items.ask: Where did Fiona and Callum fly from?
items.why: Fiona says: 'Our flight from Glasgow was eight hours.'

items.ask: How many nights are they staying?
items.why: Callum says: 'It's under MacLeod, for four nights.'
Priya says: 'Breakfast is from seven to ten in the kitchen downstairs.'

items.ask: What do Fiona and Callum love?
items.why: Callum says: 'We love music, and we'd like to see the lake.'

items.ask: How can they get to the Toronto Islands?
items.why: Priya says: 'Then take the ferry to the Toronto Islands.'

exercises.title: Speaking
exercises.intro: Think about each task. We will practise them in our lesson.
items: Role-play: a visitor arrives at your hotel, café or shop. Greet them and ask three closed questions (Is this ...? Do you ...? Would you like ... or ...?).
Now ask the same visitor three open questions (Where ...? How long ...? What ...?). Which questions got longer answers?
A tourist stops you in your town. They look lost. What do you say first? What questions do you ask to help them?
Think of a place in your town or country that tourists love. What would you tell a visitor about it: when it's open, how far it is, and what to see?

parts.rule:
Watch out

  • closed: the answer is yes or no, or one of the choices you give: Do you need a taxi? Tea or coffee?
  • open: starts with a question word, and the answer gives new information: Where are you staying?
parts.intro: Is each question closed or open? Sort them.

chips.why: The answer is yes or no: a closed question.
The answer is yes or no: a closed question.
The answer is yes or no: a closed question.
An either/or question: the visitor chooses one, so it is closed.
The answer is yes or no: a closed question.
It starts with where, and the answer is new information: an open question.
It starts with what, and invites a longer answer: an open question.
It starts with how, and the answer gives information: an open question.
It starts with who, and the answer is new information: an open question.
It starts with why, and invites a longer answer: an open question.

items.why: In a question, the helper verb comes before the subject: Where are you from?

items.q: Do you are tired after your flight?
items.why: With be, don't add do: Are you tired?
Question word + does + subject + base verb: What time does the museum open?
After did, use the base verb: Did you enjoy the tour?

items.q: How long are you staying in Canada?
items.why: Correct: question word + are + you + staying.

teacher.purpose: give students the language to welcome a visitor (as a receptionist, café or shop worker, guide, or simply a friendly local) and, above all, to ask questions correctly: closed questions (yes/no and either/or) with short answers, and open wh- questions, with the helper verb before the subject.
teacher.before: ask the student if they work (or would like to work) with tourists, and where: a hotel, a restaurant, a shop, a tour company. Print or prepare the role-play cards below, and think of one or two real places in the student's town for the speaking tasks.
plan: The three warm-up questions. Write down any questions the student says, mistakes included; you will come back to them at the end.

The welcome phrases first, then the question table. Ask the student to give you one more example of each type. Drill the short answers quickly: you ask, they answer (Are you tired? Yes, I am.). Model the intonation (see below).
Matching, then the helper verbs. After each item in Exercise 2, ask: “Why are and not do?” The rule: be and -ing forms take are/is; normal verbs take do/does/did.
Do one together and set the other for home.

The hostel conversation. Before the questions, ask the student to find Priya's questions and say which are closed and which are open (closed: Do you have a reservation? Is this your first time in Toronto? Would you like a map?; open: How was your journey? What would you like to do while you're here?). Then read it aloud together, the student as Priya.
Role-play with the cards. First round: closed questions only. Second round: open questions only. Ask the student which round felt more like a real conversation.
Exercise 7 Part A together. Go back to the questions you wrote down in the warm-up and let the student correct them. Part B at home.
pron: Intonation: yes/no questions usually rise at the end (Is this your first visit? ↗); wh- questions usually fall (Where are you from? ↘). Either/or questions rise, then fall: Tea ↗ or coffee ↘? A rising either/or sounds like a yes/no question (“tea or coffee or something else?”).
Weak forms: in fast speech do you becomes /djə/ or /dʒə/, are you /əjə/, would you /ˈwʊdʒu/, does /dəz/. Students may not hear the helper verb at all; slow down first, then model the natural speed.
journey /ˈdʒɜːni/: the first sound is /dʒ/ as in jam, and the vowel is like her, not your.
welcome /ˈwelkəm/: stress on the first syllable. reservation /ˌrezəˈveɪʃən/: stress on VA.
Short answers: the helper verb is stressed and strong in short answers: Yes, I am. /æm/, not /əm/. Negatives: isn't, aren't, don't, doesn't, didn't, with a clear /t/ at the end or a short stop.
mistakes: Statement order with a rising voice: Spanish, Italian and Portuguese speakers often make questions with intonation only: You are tired? In informal English this is possible to check something you think you heard (You're from Edinburgh?), but at work use the full form: Are you tired?

Chinese and Vietnamese speakers often keep statement order and add a question word at the end (You are from where?), because their languages use question particles. Drill the pattern: question word + helper + subject + verb.

Russian, Polish and Ukrainian speakers have no helper verbs in questions, so they often drop do: Where you live? German and French speakers may put the main verb first: Like you coffee? Both need do: Where do you live? Do you like coffee?
Double past: Did you enjoyed? Remind the student that did carries the past, so the main verb goes back to the base form.
Wrong short answer: Are you hungry? Yes, I do. The short answer repeats the helper verb of the question: are → am, do → do, can → can.
Would you like vs Do you like: Would you like a coffee? is an offer (now). Do you like coffee? asks about general taste. Students often offer things with Do you like ...?
Too direct: What's your name? or Your passport? can sound abrupt at a hotel desk. Softer: Can I have your name, please? Could I see your passport, please?

Register with customers: learners often use correct but blunt questions (What do you want? Do you want a bag?). Practise the polite forms in the “Customer service” table: Would you like ...? Could I have ...? I'm afraid .... In role-plays, ask the student to repeat a blunt question politely.
uk_us: Are you here on holiday? / Are you here on vacation?
The lift is on your left. / The elevator is on your left.
In Canada and the US the street level is the first floor. Check which system your guests know.
the check (also the bill in Canada)
Can I have the bill, please?
Please wait in the queue / in line.
adapt: Welcome phrases plus yes/no questions with are, is, do, can, would, and wh- questions with where, what, how long. Short answers with am/are/is and do.
All helper verbs, including have you been and did; add polite indirect questions (Could you tell me ...? Do you know if ...?) and follow-up questions (Oh really? What was that like?).
One role-play card at a time; the student can read the phrases from the page.
Longer role-plays with a problem: the room isn't ready, the tour is full, the guest is unhappy. The student must keep asking open questions to find a solution.
teacher.extra:
Role-play cards

Print or read these aloud. You play the visitor first; then swap.

CardHostVisitor
1. Hotel front deskWelcome the guest. Ask: reservation? how many nights? how was the journey? Give the room number and breakfast times. Offer a map.You arrive late after a long flight from Mexico City. You have a reservation for three nights. You'd like to know where to eat tonight.
2. CaféGreet the customer. Offer a table: inside or outside? Ask what they would like. Ask where they are from and what they are planning to see.You are a tourist from Australia. You want a coffee and something small to eat. You're in town for two days and want to visit a museum.
3. Helping a lost visitorYou see a visitor looking at a map. Offer help. Find out where they want to go, how they want to travel, and tell them how far it is.You are looking for the train station (or a famous place in the student's town). You have a big suitcase and you don't know if you should walk or take a taxi.
prompts: Greet a visitor and ask three closed questions. Answer with short answers that test them: “No, I'm not.” “Yes, we did.” Listen for the helper verb before the subject, and for a rising voice at the end.
Ask three open questions. Give longer answers so the student has to listen and follow up: “Oh, Edinburgh! What's it like?” Afterwards, ask which questions kept the conversation going.
Helping a lost tourist. Follow up as the tourist: “Is it far?” “Can I walk?” “How long does it take?” The student practises giving information: It's a ten-minute walk. It's open until six.
A place tourists love. Ask open questions as a curious visitor: “What can I do there?” “When is the best time to go?” “How much does it cost?” Then let the student ask you about a place in your town.

bank.why: Your room = it, in the past: Was your room comfortable?
With going (be + -ing), use are: Where are you going?

bank.q: ___ you want a table inside or on the terrace?
bank.why: Want is a normal verb, so use do with you: Do you want a table ...?

bank.q: What time ___ the shop close on Sundays?
bank.why: Close is a normal verb and the shop is it, so use does: What time does the shop close?

bank.q: Excuse me, ___ I help you find something?
bank.why: Can I help you ...? is the usual way to offer help.

bank.q: Would you like a single ___ a double room?
bank.why: An either/or question offers a choice: a single or a double?

bank.q: Are you here on holiday? Yes, I ___.
bank.why: The short answer repeats the verb of the question: Are you ...? Yes, I am.
When asks about time: When did you arrive?

bank.q: ___ are you travelling with? Your family or friends?
bank.why: Who asks about people: Who are you travelling with?

bank.q: How ___ nights would you like to stay?
bank.why: How many + plural noun asks for a number: How many nights?

bank.q: ___ you ever been to Quebec City?
bank.why: Have you ever been ...? asks about experience: present perfect.

bank.q: Did you ___ the concert last night? It was wonderful! (enjoy / enjoyed)
bank.why: After did, use the base verb: Did you enjoy ...?

bank.q: How ___ are you staying in Halifax? A week?
bank.why: How long asks about time: How long are you staying?

bank.q: Where you would like to sit?
bank.why: The helper verb comes before the subject: Where would you like to sit?
Does already has the -s, so use the base verb: Does the tour include lunch?

bank.q: Is breakfast included in the price?
bank.why: Correct: Is + subject (breakfast) + included.
With a normal verb, add do: How many bags do you have?

bank.a: What would you like to do this evening?
bank.why: Question word + would + you + like to + verb + time.

bank.a: Is this your first time in Vancouver?
bank.why: Yes/no question with be: Is + this + your first time + place?

bank.a: How did you hear about our hotel?
bank.why: Question word + did + you + base verb (hear) + about our hotel.
